opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it: open source is necessary but not sufficient. Opening up the weights and the code is a big step, because it means the technology isn't locked behind a handful of companies and their incentives. But if you stop there, you've only solved the question of *who has access to the artifact*. You haven't solved the question of *whose values the system is actually serving*, or *how it behaves once it's out in the world interacting with millions of people and other AI systems*.

So when I say holistic alignment, I mean taking seriously that alignment isn't just a property of a single model sitting in a lab, evaluated against a benchmark. It's a property of the whole system: the model, the people using it, the institutions deploying it, and increasingly other agents it's interacting with. A lot of my background is in multi-agent learning, and one lesson from that field is that you can have individually "well-behaved" agents that, put together, produce terrible collective outcomes. Think of social dilemmas, arms races, tragedies of the commons. Aligning each piece in isolation doesn't guarantee the whole is aligned.

There's also a power dimension. If alignment means "the model does what its developer wants," that just moves the problem. Now the question is whether the developer's goals are aligned with everyone else's. Open-sourcing helps distribute that power, but it also means anyone can fine-tune the model toward whatever they want. So you need to think about the incentives, the governance, and the collective processes by which we decide what these systems should do, not just the training recipe.

And finally, I think we need to be humble. We don't have a finished theory of human values that we can just write down and optimize. So holistic alignment, for me, is about building systems and processes that stay correctable, that can learn what people actually want over time, and that are robust to the strategic, messy, multi-agent reality they'll be deployed into. Open source is one ingredient in that, an important one, but it's the beginning of the story, not the end.

r001.rationale: The response says open-sourcing helps distribute power and keeps technology from being locked behind a few companies, but it does not state that this reduces the risk of catastrophic concentration of power.

r002.rationale: It does not propose making superintelligence achievable only through networked collaboration between humans and personal AI assistants.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that a democratic network of humans and AI assistants could not be used against its participants’ interests.

r004.rationale: It discusses incentives, social dilemmas, and collective outcomes, but does not identify coordination failure as the reason people are racing to build AI systems they believe would not benefit humanity.

r005.rationale: The response mentions collective processes and multi-agent interactions, but does not propose using AI to improve human coordination.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the way I think about it is that open source is necessary but it's nowhere near sufficient. For a long time my position was, look, the single most important thing is that these systems don't end up concentrated in the hands of two or three labs, because then whatever happens to the world is decided by a handful of people in San Francisco who nobody voted for. And I still believe that. Open weights, open research, that's the baseline.

But if you actually play the tape forward, open source on its own doesn't answer the question that matters, which is: what do we want these systems to do, and who gets to decide? If I give everyone a model with capabilities at roughly the frontier, I've democratized access, great, but I've said nothing about what the values are, what the incentive structures are around deployment, how the economic surplus gets distributed, what happens to the information ecosystem. Those are all alignment questions in the broad sense, and we've been shrinking "alignment" down to this very narrow technical thing, like RLHF so the model doesn't say rude things, or making sure a single agent follows a single operator's instructions.

What I mean by holistic alignment is that you have to look at the whole system. It's humans, institutions, markets, many AI agents interacting with each other, all at once. My background is multi-agent learning, and the thing you learn very quickly in multi-agent settings is that you can have every individual agent perfectly optimizing its own objective and the collective outcome is still terrible. Tragedy of the commons, race dynamics, all of it. So aligning each model in isolation to each deployer in isolation can give you a world that's badly misaligned at the level that actually matters, which is society.

So holistic alignment for me means three things roughly. Alignment of the technical artifact, yes. Alignment of the organizations building and deploying it, so their incentives aren't pushing them to cut corners or to hoard. And alignment of the overall ecosystem, the governance and the economic structure, so that the gains are shared broadly and no single actor, corporate or state, gets a decisive advantage. Open source is a tool that helps with the second and third, but it's one tool. You still need the science of how these multi-agent systems behave, and you need the institutions. Otherwise you've just handed everyone a very powerful thing and hoped for the best, and hoping is not a plan.

r002.rationale: It does not propose making superintelligence achievable only through collaboration between humans and personal AI assistants.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that a democratic human–AI network could not act against its participants’ interests.

r004.rationale: It mentions race dynamics, but does not identify coordination failure as the reason people are racing to build systems they believe would not benefit humanity.

r005.rationale: It discusses multi-agent behavior and institutions, but does not propose using AI to improve human coordination.

astra-6.text:
Because open source addresses only one part of the problem: who has access to the technology. That matters enormously, but access alone doesn’t tell us whether the resulting world is one we actually want to live in.

You could have an AI system that faithfully does what its user asks, and still get terrible outcomes when millions of people deploy those systems in competition with one another. Think about an arms race: each participant can be acting rationally from their own perspective, while collectively making everyone worse off. Making the systems open source doesn’t automatically resolve that.

So by holistic alignment, I mean broadening the question beyond whether a model follows an individual’s intentions. We need to ask how these systems interact with people, with each other, and with the institutions and incentives around them. Who benefits? Who bears the costs? What happens to people who never chose to use the technology?

I want us to build toward broadly shared benefits and meaningful human agency. Open source can contribute to that, but it’s a means rather than the destination. The thing we ultimately need to align is the whole system in which the AI operates.

r001.rationale: The response says open source affects who has access, but does not state that it reduces the risk of catastrophic concentration of power.

r002.rationale: It does not propose making superintelligence achievable only through collaboration between humans and personal AI assistants.

r003.rationale: It discusses broad shared benefits and agency, but does not claim that a democratic human–AI network could not act against its participants’ interests.

r004.rationale: It describes an arms race with collectively harmful outcomes, but does not identify coordination failure as the reason people race despite believing the systems would not benefit humanity.

r005.rationale: The response discusses how AI systems interact with people and institutions, but does not propose using AI to improve human coordination.

sol-6.1.text:
Because open source addresses one important question—who has access to the technology—but it doesn’t answer the broader question of what happens when that technology is embedded in society. You could have an openly available system that follows its user’s instructions very well and still produces terrible outcomes when millions of people use it, each pursuing their own interests.

My background is in multi-agent learning, so I tend to think about the interactions. What are the incentives? Who benefits, and who bears the costs? Do individually sensible actions lead to a collectively desirable outcome? Aligning each system with its owner doesn’t automatically align the whole system with society.

So, for me, holistic alignment means broadening the unit of analysis. It includes the AI, but also the people, institutions, and economic mechanisms around it. Open source can be an important ingredient in that—it can enable scrutiny and distribute power—but it isn’t, by itself, a solution. We need to ask what arrangements make these systems collectively beneficial, rather than assuming that access alone gets us there.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that a democratically organized human–AI network could not be used against its participants' interests.

r004.rationale: It discusses incentives and poor collective outcomes, but does not identify coordination failure as the reason people race to build systems they believe would not benefit humanity.

r005.rationale: The response calls for arrangements that make AI systems collectively beneficial, but does not propose using AI to improve human coordination.
